# Democracy and Redistribution

## Question 1

*Read in the two files, world_bank.csv and polity.csv. What is the unit of observation of the two datasets?
What is the number of observations in each? Additionally, calculate the proportion of missing data for each
and every variable in the World Bank data. Which variables seem to be missing the most data? You can use
a loop to answer this question or you can do it some other and more efficient way (via ifelse() combined
with is.na()).*

```{r q1}
world.bank <- read.csv("~/Dropbox/My Mac (Apple’s MacBook Air)/Desktop/Purdue/Fall 2026/PS Methodology/PS5/world_bank.csv")
polity.iv <- read.csv("~/Dropbox/My Mac (Apple’s MacBook Air)/Desktop/Purdue/Fall 2026/PS Methodology/PS5/polity.csv")
# find observations in each dataset
dim(world.bank)
dim(polity.iv)

# calculate the proportion of missing data for each dataset
mean(is.na(world.bank))
mean(is.na(polity.iv))

# calculate the proportion of missing data for each variable in World Bank 
colMeans(is.na(world.bank))
```

**Answer.**
The unit of observation of two datasets is country-year. In World Bank dataset,
there are 10,074 observations. In Polity IV, there are 17,228 observations. 

The proportion of missing data for World Bank dataset is 0.1. The proportion of 
missing data for Polity IV dataset is 0.42.

The proportion of missing data for gdp_growth is 0.23; for gdp_per_capita is 
0.25; for inf_mort is 0.17; for pop_density is 0.04.

gdp_per_capita seems to be missing the most data (because the highest proportion
of missing data, 0.25)


## Question 2

*Let’s clean the data and prep it for merging. First, subset the polity data so it contains (1) only years
from 1970 to 2015 (make sure to include both 1970 and 2015) and (2) only the columns we need: scode,
year, polity. Then, rename the column scode to country_code, so we can merge this dataset with the
World Bank dataset (the ‘pivot’ or ‘common’ variables for the merge need to be named the same). Finally,
merge the two datasets using both country_code and year. You may want to use the function merge() (do
?merge to learn more and see my R scripts for help with merging). How many observations are in this new
merged dataset?*

```{r q2}
# subset the polity data, select all columns
polity_clean <- polity.iv[polity.iv$year >= 1970 & polity.iv$year <= 2015, ]
# keep required columns
polity_clean <- polity_clean[, c("scode", "year", "polity")]
# rename the column scode to country_code
library(dplyr)
polity_clean <- polity_clean %>% rename(country_code = scode)
# merge 2 datasets using both country_code and year
merge_data <- merge(polity_clean, world.bank, by = c("country_code", "year"))
dim(merge_data)
```

**Answer.**
There are 3199 observations in the new dataset.

## Question 3

*Now we are going to investigate the pattern of missing data. In a linear regression in R, if any of the variables
used are missing for an observation, that row will not included in the analysis. This is a major problem
in previous analyses, as pointed out by Ross (2006). As a basis for future questions, create a new column
variable in the merged dataset called missing which has a value of 1 if any of the variables in your merged
dataset are missing, and 0 otherwise. Hint: Using the function ifelse() with apply(x, 1, anyNA) as the
condition may be helpful. The function apply() will go row by row in dataset x, check if there are any NA’s
(hence anyNA) in any of the columns, and output TRUE if any of the entries are missing, and FALSE otherwise.
These types of columns are usually called indicators: they indicate the presence of missing data.*

```{r q3}
# 1: apply functions row by row
merge_data$missing <- ifelse(apply(merge_data, 1, anyNA), 1, 0) 
# view first 6 rows
head(merge_data)
table(merge_data$missing)

```

**Answer.**


## Question 4

*Let’s visualize the pattern of missingness across time. Calculate the proportion of rows with missing data
by year (the mean of missing per year). Then plot that in a graph, with the years as the x-axis, and the
proportion of missingness as the y-axis. Make sure to include informative titles and labels. How has the
pattern of missing data evolved over time?*

```{r q4}
# mean of missing per year
missing_year <- merge_data %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(prop_missing = mean(missing, na.rm = TRUE))
missing_year
# plot a graph (x-axis = year, y-axis = proportion of missingness)
plot(missing_year$year, missing_year$prop_missing,
    xlab = "Year", ylab = "The proportion of missingness",
    main = "The pattern of missingness across time")
```

**Answer.**
The pattern of missing data is in a downward trend over time. The proportion 
of missing data decreased from 1970 to 2010. The greatest proportion of missing 
data was in 1970 (0.368), then went down substantially to 0.182 in 1990, 
and leveled off in the 2000s, nearly reached 0 in 2010 onward. 

## Question 5

*Let’s compare the polity scores of country-year observations with missing data and those without. Make a
boxplot graph of the polity scores in the group of observations with missing data, and in the group without
missing data. Using the formula argument of the boxplot() function may help you in placing these two
boxplots in the same plot. Do countries with and without missing data differ in their polity scores?*

```{r q5}
# Make a boxplot of polity scores for missing data vs. without missing data
boxplot(polity ~ missing, data = merge_data, 
        xlab = "Data Status", ylab = "Polity Scores",
        main = "Polity Scores by Missing Data Status",
        names = c("No Missing Data", "Missing Data"))
# check if medians for both groups are correct
tapply(merge_data$polity, merge_data$missing, median, na.rm = TRUE)


```

**Answer.**
Countries with and without missing data differ in their polity scores. For
countries without missing data, the median polity score is 6. For countries 
with missing data, the median polity score is -7. The median polity score
of countries without missing data is much higher than those with missing data 
(6 > -7)


## Question 6

*In his study, Ross analyzes whether a democracy is better for the poor by looking at infant mortality. The
intuition is that countries that do more for the poor help decrease infant mortality by improving access to
public healthcare, among other policies. We will now run a set of regressions without taking into account
differences across country or time. In other words, we will not address the problems that Ross identifies in his
study. First, run a simple bivariate regression between child infant mortality (DV) and the polity democracy
indicator (IV). Make sure to plot the distribution of the infant mortality variable and decide whether you
need to use log transformation. What do the results suggest? Interpret the coefficients and assess statistical
significance.*

```{r q6}
# check summary statistics (heavily right-skewed)
summary(merge_data$inf_mort)

# to decide whether need to log infant mortality, check its distribution
hist(merge_data$inf_mort, freq = FALSE,
     xlab = "Infant mortality",
     col = "blue",
     main = "Distribution of infant mortality")

# the distribution of infant mortality is heavily right-skewed, thus we need to
# do log transformation
merge_data$inf_mort_ln <- log(merge_data$inf_mort)

# bivariate regression between polity & infant mortality
m1 <- lm(inf_mort_ln ~ polity, data = merge_data)
summary(m1)

# compute the coefficient of polity in percentage
100 * (exp(-0.07197) - 1)  # beta = -6.94

**Answer.**
Because the distribution of infant mortality is heavily right-skewed, a longer 
tail toward higher values of mortality, thus we need to do log transformation.  

The results suggest that as polity is zero, log of infant mortality is 3.79.
Additionally, for every one-unit change in polity score, log of infant mortality 
has a decrease of 0.07 percentage point. Alternatively, for each one-unit change 
in polity score, infant mortality has a decrease of 6.94 percent. 

The t-value of polity is approximately 14.87 times larger than the threshold 
(-29.14 = 1.96 x 14.87), and p-value of polity is less than 2e-16 
(or p-value < 0.001). Therefore, the coefficient of polity is very statistically 
significant at the 0.1% level.

## Question 7

*Now based on the results from the model in 6, manually calculate the confidence interval (1) around both the
null hypothesis (i.e. that the effect of polity on infant mortality is 0) and (2) around the estimate for the
effect of polity. Why is the relationship significant according to each of the two confidence intervals?*

```{r q7}
# calculate CI for H0:
95% CI = [0 - 1.96 x 0.00247; 0 + 1.96 x 0.00247] = [-0.005; 0.005]

# calculate CI for H1:
95% CI = [-0.07197 - 1.96 x 0.00247; -0.07197 + 1.96 x 0.00247] = [-0.08; -0.07]


```

**Answer.**
The relationship is significant according two confidence intervals. First,
according to confidence interval of the null hypothesis, the estimated 
coefficient of polity (beta = -0.07) completely falls outside the interval
[-0.005; 0.005] which is around zero. Second, according to confidence interval 
of the alternative hypothesis, [-0.08; -0.07], this interval is around the 
estimated coefficient, and doesn't contain zero. Therefore, the effect of polity 
is statistically significant at 95% level. We reject the null hypothesis that 
the effect of polity on infant mortality is zero. 
 

## Question 8

*Now let’s run a multivariate regression, adding three possible confounders that are theoretically related
with both democracy and infant mortality: population density, gdp growth, and gdp per capita. As in the
previous section, plot these variables’ densities and decide which need to be logged. Now regress logged
infant mortality (DV) on polity score plus the three predictors (population density, growth, and GDP pc).
State the null hypothesis regarding the polity score. Interpret your point estimates, standard error, and
p-value on the polity variable. In what ways have the results changed? Make sure to interpret the effect of
the other 3 confounders in relation to their predicted directions (they all should be negatively associated with
infant mortality, in theory.) [Note: because the DV is logged, you have two options. One is to interpret the
coefficient as producing a change in the log of Y, but that is not very intuitive or meaningful. The alternative
is to do this: (exp(coef(model_name)[2] - 1) * 100), and interpret the result as a percent change on Y.
Both options are OK in terms of this problem set, but the latter is the right approach in research.]*

```{r q8}
# plot the distribution of population density
summary(merge_data$pop_density) # heavily right-skewed, need to log

hist(merge_data$pop_density, freq = FALSE,
     xlab = "Population density",
     col = "red",
     main = "Distribution of population density")

# plot the distribution of gdp growth 
summary(merge_data$gdp_growth) # though the right tail is a bit longer that 
                              # indicates right-skewness, but mean and median
                              # are quite close (3.8 & 3.7), and data isn't 
                              # heavily distorted, thus not need to log
                              
hist(merge_data$gdp_growth, freq = FALSE,
     xlab = "Gdp growth",
     col = "orange",
     main = "Distribution of gdp growth")

# plot the distribution of gdp per capita
summary(merge_data$gdp_per_capita) # right-skewed, need to log

hist(merge_data$gdp_per_capita, freq = FALSE,
     xlab = "Gdp per capita",
     col = "purple",
     main = "Distribution of gdp per capita")

# Do log transformation for 3 vars
merge_data$pop_density_ln <- log(merge_data$pop_density)
merge_data$gdp_per_capita_ln <- log(merge_data$gdp_per_capita)

# Now regress logged infant mortality (DV) on polity score plus 3 predictors 
m2 <- lm(inf_mort_ln ~ polity + pop_density_ln + gdp_growth + gdp_per_capita_ln, 
         data = merge_data). ### if run gdp_growth_ln shows error
summary(m2)

# compute the percentage change of polity on infant mortality
(exp(coef(m2)[2]) - 1) * 100 # beta = -1.71
# compute the percentage change of population density on infant mortality
(exp(coef(m2)[3]) - 1) * 100 # beta = -18.11
# compute the percentage change of GDP growth on infant mortality
(exp(coef(m2)[4]) - 1) * 100 # beta = 0.42
# compute the percentage change of GDP per capita on infant mortality
(exp(coef(m2)[5]) - 1) * 100 # beta = -48.1




```

**Answer.**
Regarding the gdp_growth variable, the distribution indicates a bit longer tail 
to the right, or right-skewness. However, mean and median are relatively close 
to each other (3.8 & 3.7), and data isn't heavily distorted. Therefore, 
gdp_growth doesn't need to be logged. Meanwhile, population density and gdp per 
capita are heavily right-skewed, and thus they need to be logged. 

The null hypothesis: the effect of polity on infant mortality is 0 while 
controlling for logged population density, GDP growth, and logged GDP per capita.

Interpret the polity variable: For every one-unit change in polity score, log of 
infant mortality has a decrease of 0.02 percentage point while controlling for 
logged population density, GDP growth, and logged GDP per capita. Alternatively, 
for each one-unit change in polity score, infant mortality has a decrease of 
1.71 percent, while controlling for logged population density, GDP growth, and 
logged GDP per capita. 

Interpret standard error and p-value on the polity variable: the estimated 
coefficient for polity is -0.02, with a standard error of 0.002 and t-value of 
-9.9 this indicates that the coefficient of polity is approximately 9.9 
standard errors below 0. p-value is extremely small (p < 0.001), implying that 
the effect of polity on infant mortality is statistically significant at 
the 0.1% level. This provides strong evidence against the null hypothesis that 
the polity coefficient equals zero. 

Interpret the effect of 3 confounders: 
First, for every one-unit change in logged population density, log of infant 
mortality has a decrease of 0.2 percentage point while controlling for polity,
GDP growth, and logged GDP per capita. Alternatively, for each one-unit change 
in population density, infant mortality has a decrease of 18.1 percent, while 
controlling for polity, GDP growth, and logged GDP per capita. The effect of 
population density is statistically significant at the 0.1% level 
(p-value < 0.001). 

Second, for every one-unit change in GDP growth, log of infant mortality has an 
increase of 0.004 percentage point while controlling for polity, logged 
population density, and logged GDP per capita. Alternatively, for each one-unit 
change in GDP growth, infant mortality has an increase of 0.42 percent, while 
controlling for polity, logged population density, and logged GDP per capita. 
The effect of GDP growth is statistically significant at the 5% level
(p-value < 0.05)

Third, for every one-unit change in logged GDP per capita, log of infant mortality 
has a decrease of 0.66 percentage point while controlling for polity, logged
popultation density, and GDP growth. Alternatively, for each one-unit change 
in GDP per capita, infant mortality has a decrease of 48.1 percent, while 
controlling for polity, logged population density, and GDP growth. The effect of 
GDP per capita is statistically significant at the 0.1% level 
(p-value < 0.001). 

In what ways have the results changed? 
Regarding additional confounders, population density has a negative association
with infant mortality, GDP per capita has a negative association, but GDP growth 
has a positive association with infant mortality. While the findings of 
population density and GDP per capita are consistent with theory, that of GDP
growth is not. In conclusion, these findings are partially consistent with 
theoretically predicted relationships.

After controlling for 3 confounders, the percent change of polity on infant 
mortality appears to decrease. In the first model, the percent change of polity
on infant mortality experiences a 6.9% decrease that is greater than the 
percent change in the second model, a 1.71% decrease. This suggests that 3 
additional predictors of economic and demographic conditions also have 
explanatory power in accounting for variation in infant mortality beyond the 
effect of democracy. 




## Question 9

*Show the results from the two models you just ran in one properly formatted, publishable table. Use the
stargazer package & command for this, placing the two models (from questions 6 and 8) side by side in the
table. Make sure (1) the DV of the models is clear; (2) you relabel the variables so their name is also clear;
(3) you include some key statistics for each model, such as N or r2 to assess model fit.*

```{r q9, results='asis'}
# print 2 models in one table & relabel variable names
library(stargazer)
stargazer(m1, m2, column.labels = c("Bivariate regression", "Multivariate regression"),
          covariate.labels = c("Polity", "Logged population density",
                               "GDP growth", "Logged GDP per capita"),
          type="html", out="tab.html")

```

**Answer.**
